units.translation: [It is said in the masculine gender ὁ σκότος [darkness] or in the neuter τὸ σκότος [darkness]. The masculine is attributed to the Attic writers by Aelius Dionysius in Eustathius p. 1390, 56 and other grammarians, except that Photius p. 525, 4 noted σκότος καὶ σκότον ἑκατέρως· οὕτως Ἀμειψίας [darkness and darkness in both ways; thus Ameipsias], and Lysippus in Dicaearchus' Description of Greece p. 22 Buttm. said τοιοῦτο τῶν ξένων τι καταχεῖται σκότος [such a darkness of the strangers pours over] because the meter demanded it. But in Aristophanes it is never read otherwise than in the masculine form, nor is there any evidence for the neuter form among the tragedians, as L. Dindorf showed in the Thesaurus vol. 7 p. 446 after examining the examples of the neuter form that were formerly cited. Plato, however, Xenophon, and other prose writers, unless the books are entirely deceptive, seem to have used both forms, as was shown by the examples adduced in the Thesaurus loc. cit., although even in these authors it is uncertain which examples are due to the scribes and which to the writers themselves.] darkness, gloom.
Thus Scaliger corrected what is written in M as ὁ δυσφιλής κότῳ [the hostile one with anger].
